item.description: Visa is running an RFP for a new stablecoin settlement partner after Mastercard closed its $1.8bn purchase of BVNK — the network's own supplier now belongs to its rival. Plus SAMA's governor takes an FSB regional chair, Saudi banks post a record Q2, and HSBC and Standard Chartered move the first live tokenised deposit across Swift's blockchain ledger. # Ep. 06 — Visa's Missing Partner and the Master Merchant Model **Wednesday 26 August 2026 · Riyadh**
## Cold open — the networks buy the plumbing Visa is looking for a new stablecoin settlement partner with licensing across the US, Canada, the UK and Singapore, per documents reported by CoinDesk. The role was previously BVNK's — Mastercard announced the up-to-$1.8bn acquisition in March and closed it on 3 August. The RFP covers coin swaps, settlement, OTC and support for **Open USD**, the multi-coin project fronted by Stripe, Visa and Mastercard.
## Saudi - **SAMA governor Ayman Al-Sayari** appointed the Financial Stability Board's **Regional Engagement Chair**, two-year term from 10 August 2026. - **Record Q2**: the ten listed Saudi banks reported combined net profit of SAR 24.87bn (~$6.63bn), up 12.5% YoY. Riyad Bank's Q2 net income of SAR 2.6bn beat United Securities' SAR 2.4bn estimate; NSCI +5.5% to SAR 3.38bn. - **Riyad Bank AT1 sukuk** concluded 3 August: SAR 13.6bn of orders, ~300% coverage, issue upsized to SAR 10bn. - **Fintech base**: licensed fintechs up from 80 (2022) to 280+ by mid-2025; Fintech Saudi targets 525 licensed firms and $3.5bn GDP contribution by 2030. Q1 2026's five most-funded Saudi startups were all fintech, raising $86.3m between them. - **Open banking**: SAMA began licensing open banking providers in March 2026 after the sandbox; Lean Technologies took the first licence. - **GCC**: Fintech Galaxy received in-principle approval from CBUAE as an open finance provider, enabling participation in **Al Tareq**, the UAE open finance scheme. Full authorisation timeline not published.
## Global - **Tokenised deposits go live**: HSBC and Standard Chartered executed the first live cross-border tokenised deposit transaction on Swift's blockchain-based ledger on 19 August. Obligations recorded on each bank's own tokenised deposit infrastructure; Swift's ledger acted as orchestration/netting layer, with final settlement through existing systems. Pilot spans 17 banks across six continents; currencies include AED. - **GENIUS Act**: US Treasury proposed the implementing rules defining who may issue, offer and sell payment stablecoins — issuance ban effective 18 January 2027, offer-and-sale cutoff for unlicensed issuers July 2028; the OCC's rule to be final by November. FASB has proposed stablecoin accounting treatment. - **AI/M&A**: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter reported at over $7bn. Klarna cut guidance and the stock fell 19%. - **Agentic payments**: Token Terminal counted 8.7m x402 stablecoin transfers in the week starting 17 August — the busiest week of the year, on very small dollar value.
## Product explained — Payment facilitation (the master merchant model) **What it is.** A platform signs one merchant agreement with an acquirer, takes a single master merchant ID, and onboards businesses beneath it as *sub-merchants*. The sub-merchant contracts with the platform, not the bank.
**Problem solved.** Traditional merchant onboarding (CR, VAT certificate, ownership, risk review, MCC, terminal) takes days to weeks. PayFac collapses it to minutes inside the software the merchant already uses — and turns a fixed SaaS fee into a share of payment volume.
**Money flow.** Issuer authorises → scheme clears → acquirer settles **gross to the master merchant** → platform splits in its own sub-ledger (interchange, scheme fees, platform margin, reserves, refunds) → payout to each sub-merchant's IBAN.
**Risk.** Chargebacks land on the master MID; the platform is liable to the acquirer and recovers from the sub-merchant. Future-delivery exposure (deposits taken now, service later) is the core risk — hence reserves and rolling holdbacks. The bank's risk stops being diversified across thousands of merchants and concentrates in one counterparty.
**Providers.** Global: Stripe Connect, Adyen for Platforms, Square, Shopify, Toast, Lightspeed. Enablers: Finix, Infinicept, Payrix (Worldpay). Merchant-of-record: Paddle, FastSpring. Saudi/GCC: Foodics, Geidea, HyperPay, Moyasar, PayTabs, Telr, Tap; commerce platforms Salla and Zid.
**The SAMA line.** SAMA's *Rules for Dealing with E-Commerce Payment Service and Support Providers* treat linkage and technical support as supporting services that do not require a SAMA licence — technical permits come from Saudi Payments. Explicitly outside that: contracting directly with merchants; registering them and verifying data for KYC/AML/CFT and counter-fraud; finalising settlement; depositing funds into the merchant's bank account. The *Implementing Regulations of the Payments and Payment Services Law* define **Payment Aggregation Service** as facilitating payment on a pooled basis.
**Bank/PSP checklist.** Master merchant agreement with enforceable indemnity and callable reserve · API-based sub-merchant onboarding (register lookup, UBOs, sanctions screening) · sub-merchant-level risk monitoring · segregated settlement so merchant funds sit outside the platform's estate · dispute routing with evidence · portability/exit plan · right to inspect and right to suspend, in writing.
